title: Theorem

\label{thm:equitableValency}
    Let $\Gamma \in \mathscr{G}_3(\theta_0,\theta_1,\theta_2)$ have at most three distinct degrees. Then the degree partition $\mathfrak{D}(\Gamma)$ is equitable, and $\theta_0$ is an eigenvalue of the quotient matrix $Q_{\mathfrak{D}(\Gamma)}(\Gamma)$.

label: eq:BBstar
title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:equitableValency} the degree-partition is equitable.
Hence, $B\mathbf1_{n_2}=k_{12}\mathbf1_{n_1}$ and $B^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\mathbf1_{n_1}=k_{21}\mathbf1_{n_2}$.
The $(1,1)$-block of \eqref{eqn:3ev} is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BBstar}
BB^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 

   =-A_1^2+(\theta_1+\theta_2) A_1-\theta_1\theta_2I+\alpha_1^2J,
\end{equation}
where $\alpha_1^2=k_{11}+k_{12}+\theta_1\theta_2$.
In the complete multipartite case, $A_1=J-I_m\otimes J_n$ and $A_1^2=(n_1-2n)J+n(I_m\otimes J_n)$.
In the disjoint-union-of-cliques case, $A_1=I_m\otimes J_n-I$ and $A_1^2=I+(n-2)(I_m\otimes J_n)$.
Substitution in \eqref{eq:BBstar} yields
\[
BB^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 

   =k_{12}I+\lambda_1(I_m\otimes J_n-I)+\lambda_2(J-I_m\otimes J_n),
\]
with the values of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ given by \eqref{eqn:l1l2}.
Since $B$ is a $\{0,1\}$-matrix with constant row and column sums, this proves the GDD assertion.

For the rest of the proof, assume that $\mathcal D$ is semiregular.
On the $(m-1)$-dimensional space of vectors that are constant on each group and orthogonal to $\mathbf1_{n_1}$, the eigenvalue of $BB^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
$ is
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:beta}
    \beta=k_{12}+(n-1)\lambda_1-n\lambda_2.
\end{equation}
Using semiregularity and \eqref{eqn:gdd}, we have $\beta=k_{12}k_{21}-n_1\lambda_2=0$.
On the other hand, substituting \eqref{eqn:l1l2} into \eqref{eqn:beta} yields
\[
\beta=
\begin{cases}
-(n+\theta_1)(n+\theta_2),
    &\text{if $\Gamma[V_1]=\overline{mK_n}$},\\
-\bigl(n-1-\theta_1\bigr)\bigl(n-1-\theta_2\bigr),
    &\text{if $\Gamma[V_1]=mK_n$}.
\end{cases}
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:rank-one}, we have $\theta_1\geqslant0$ and $\theta_2<0$.
Furthermore, since $n\geqslant2$, the factors $n+\theta_1$ and $n-1-\theta_2$ are positive.
Consequently, $n=-\theta_2$ in the first case and $n=\theta_1+1$ in the second.

Since $n_1k_{12}=n_2k_{21}$, we have
\[
    \bigl(B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2}\bigr)
        \mathbf1_{n_2}=0,
    \qquad
    \bigl(B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2}\bigr)^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 

        \mathbf1_{n_1}=0.
\]
The vanishing of $\beta$ shows that $B^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
$ annihilates every vector orthogonal to $\mathbf1_{n_1}$ that is constant on each group.
Therefore, the sum of the incidence rows in any group is independent of the group, whence $(I_m \otimes J_n)B=(k_{21}/m)J$ and hence $(I_m \otimes J_n)\bigl(B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2}\bigr)=0$.
Thus,
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:A1J}
    A_1\bigl(B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2}\bigr)
=a\bigl(B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2}\bigr),
\end{equation}
where $a=0$ in the complete multipartite case and $a=-1$ in the disjoint-union-of-cliques case.
The $(1,2)$-block of \eqref{eqn:3ev} is
\[
A_1B+BA_2-(\theta_1+\theta_2) B=\alpha_1\alpha_2J.
\]
Using \eqref{eqn:A1J}, we obtain
\[
\bigl(B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2}\bigr)A_2
=(\theta_1+\theta_2-a)\bigl(B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2}\bigr),
\]
and transposing yields,
\[
A_2\bigl(B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2}\bigr)^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 

=(\theta_1+\theta_2-a)\bigl(B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2}\bigr)^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
.
\]
Thus $A_2$ acts as the scalar $\theta_1+\theta_2-a$ on $\operatorname{Im}\bigl((B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2})^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\bigr)$.
Moreover,
\[
\mathbb R^{n_2}
 =\langle\mathbf1_{n_2}\rangle
   \oplus\operatorname{Im}\bigl((B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2})^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\bigr)
   \oplus\ker B
\]
is an orthogonal decomposition.
Indeed, $k_{21}>0$ by connectedness, and the row space of $B$ is $\langle\mathbf1_{n_2}\rangle\oplus \operatorname{Im}\bigl((B-\frac{k_{21}}{n_1}J_{n_1,n_2})^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\bigr)$.
These subspaces are invariant under the symmetric matrix $A_2$.
Since $\ker B\subseteq\mathbf1_{n_2}^{\perp}$ the $(2,2)$-block of \eqref{eqn:3ev} restricted to $\ker B$ yields
\[
(A_2-\theta_1I)(A_2-\theta_2I)=0.
\]
The eigenvalues of $A_2$ therefore belong to $\{k_{22},\theta_1+\theta_2-a,\theta_1,\theta_2\}$.

label: rem:semireg
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:semireg}
    Semiregular GDDs have the property that every block intersects every group in the same number of points.
    Since $\mathcal{D}$ is a semiregular GDD, every block intersects every group in exactly $k/m$ points. 
    This implies $(I_m \otimes J_n) B = \frac{k}{m} J_{v,b}$. 
Thus, $X_{\mathcal D} B = (J_v - I_m \otimes J_n) B = k J_{v,b} - \frac{k}{m} J_{v,b} = \frac{k(m-1)}{m} J_{v,b}$.
head: environment

label: thm:gdd-to-3ev
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eqn:1p
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathcal D$ is semiregular, \eqref{eqn:gdd} becomes $r-\lambda_1=n(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)>0$.
In particular, $\lambda_2-\lambda_1>0$ and $k>0$.
We can rearrange \eqref{eqn:aux-mixed} as
\[
    \left(B-\frac{k}{v}J_{v,b} \right)A(\Gamma)= \left(\lambda_2-\lambda_1-n \right) \left( B-\frac{k}{v}J_{v,b} \right).
\]
Since $(B-\frac{k}{v}J_{v,b})$ is nonzero, $\lambda_2-\lambda_1-n$ is an eigenvalue of $A(\Gamma)$, and $\lambda_2-\lambda_1-n \leqslant k_\Gamma$.
Therefore,
\[
    C\coloneqq\frac{k(m-1)}{m}
          +\frac{k}{v}(k_\Gamma-\lambda_2+\lambda_1+n)
      =\frac{k}{v}(v+k_\Gamma-\lambda_2+\lambda_1)
      \geqslant\frac{k}{v}(v-n)>0.
\]
Since $v-n+\lambda_1>0$, we apply \eqref{eqn:aux-scalar} to deduce $d\coloneqq\frac{1}{b}
       \big((k_\Gamma-\lambda_2+\lambda_1)(k_\Gamma+n)+rk\big)>0$.
We may therefore set
\[
    \alpha_1=\sqrt{v-n+\lambda_1},\qquad
    \alpha_2=\sqrt d
\]
and \eqref{eqn:aux-scalar} implies $\alpha_1\alpha_2=C$.
Let $A=\left [\begin{smallmatrix}X_{\mathcal D}&B\\
                       B^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
&A(\Gamma)\end{smallmatrix}\right ]$.
We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:1p}
    A^2-(\lambda_2-\lambda_1-n) A-n(\lambda_2-\lambda_1) I
       =\begin{bmatrix}
          \alpha_1^2J_v&\alpha_1\alpha_2J_{v,b}\\
          \alpha_1\alpha_2J_{b,v}&\alpha_2^2J_b
        \end{bmatrix}.
\end{equation}

We have $X_{\mathcal D}=J_v-I_m\otimes J_n$, so $X_{\mathcal D}^2=(v-2n)J_v+nI_m\otimes J_n$ and
\[
BB^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
=(r-\lambda_1)I_v-(\lambda_2-\lambda_1) I_m\otimes J_n+\lambda_2J_v.
\]
Using $r-\lambda_1=n(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)$, the $(1,1)$-block of the left-hand side of \eqref{eqn:1p} is therefore $(v-n+\lambda_1)J_v=\alpha_1^2J_v$.
By Remark~\ref{rem:semireg} and \eqref{eqn:aux-mixed}, the $(1,2)$-block of left-hand side of \eqref{eqn:1p} is
\[
    X_{\mathcal D}B+BA(\Gamma)-(\lambda_2-\lambda_1-n) B=CJ_{v,b}
       =\alpha_1\alpha_2J_{v,b}.
\]
The $(2,1)$-block follows by transposition, and the $(2,2)$-block is exactly \eqref{eqn:aux-block}.  
This proves \eqref{eqn:1p}.

The complete multipartite graph on the point vertices is connected, since $m\geqslant2$, and every block vertex has $k>0$ point neighbours.
Hence the graph with adjacency matrix $A$ is connected.
Set $\bm\alpha^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
 = [\alpha_1\mathbf1_v^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
,\alpha_2\mathbf1_b^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
]$.
Then \eqref{eqn:1p} becomes
\[
    (A-(\lambda_2-\lambda_1) I)(A+nI)=\bm\alpha\bm\alpha^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
.
\]
Since $A$ commutes with the right-hand side, it preserves $\langle\bm\alpha\rangle$.
The Perron--Frobenius theorem~\cite[Theorem 2.2.1]{BrouwerHaemers2012} therefore identifies $\bm\alpha$ as a Perron eigenvector, with simple eigenvalue $\theta_0$.
On $\bm\alpha^\perp$, we have $(A-(\lambda_2-\lambda_1) I)(A+nI) = O$, so all remaining eigenvalues belong to $\{\lambda_2-\lambda_1,-n\}$.
Both must occur, otherwise $A$ would have a quadratic minimal polynomial, forcing $(A^2)_{xy}=0$ for every pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices $x,y$.  
However, two distinct point vertices in the same group are nonadjacent and have at least $v-n>0$ common neighbours.
Moreover,
\[
    (\theta_0-\lambda_2+\lambda_1)(\theta_0+n)=\|\bm\alpha\|^2>0,
\]
and $\theta_0>0$, so $\theta_0>\lambda_2-\lambda_1$.

The point--block partition is equitable, with quotient matrix
\[
    Q=\begin{bmatrix}v-n&r\\k&k_\Gamma\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Its positive eigenvector $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
$ has eigenvalue $\theta_0$, which is therefore the larger root of its characteristic polynomial.  
Thus
\[
    \theta_0=
       \frac{v-n+k_\Gamma+
          \sqrt{(v-n-k_\Gamma)^2+4rk}}{2}.
\]
The row sums of $Q$ are $v-n+r$ and $k_\Gamma+k$, respectively.
These give the two vertex degrees, proving the final assertion.
head: environment

label: rem:degree-compatibility
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:degree-compatibility}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:gdd-to-3ev}, set $\theta_1=\lambda_2-\lambda_1$ and $\theta_2=-n$.
The diagonal entries of \eqref{eqn:aux-block}, together with \eqref{eqn:aux-scalar}, imply
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:degree-compatibility}
    \frac{k^2}{v^2}(v+k_\Gamma-\theta_1)^2
       =(v-n+\lambda_1)(k_\Gamma+k+\theta_1\theta_2).
\end{equation}
The point--block partition is equitable, with quotient matrix $Q=\left [ \begin{smallmatrix}v-n&r\\k&k_\Gamma\end{smallmatrix}\right ]$.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:gdd-to-3ev} and the spectral inclusion for equitable quotients, its nonprincipal eigenvalue is $\theta\in\{\theta_1,\theta_2\}$, so $(v-n-\theta)(k_\Gamma-\theta)=rk=v\lambda_2$.
Consequently, the candidate degrees are
\[
    k_\Gamma=\lambda_2-n\quad\text{if }\theta=\theta_2,
    \qquad
    k_\Gamma=\theta_1+\frac{v\lambda_2}{v-n-\theta_1}
       \quad\text{if }\theta=\theta_1.
\]
In the second case, $v-n>\theta_1$, since the smaller eigenvalue of $Q$ is less than either diagonal entry.  
Each candidate must also satisfy \eqref{eqn:degree-compatibility}.

label: rem:OA
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:OA}
    The first and fourth rows of Table~\ref{tab:feasible-parameters} both have $\lambda_1 = 0$ and $k = m$, so every block of each is a transversal of the groups by     Remark~\ref{rem:semireg}; that is, their designs are \textbf{transversal designs}, or equivalently \textbf{orthogonal arrays of strength $2$}: arrays over an $n$-set in which every ordered pair of symbols occurs equally often in every pair of columns (see~\cite[Part~III]{handbookCD}).
    The first row requires an $\mathrm{OA}(54,4,3,2)$ and the fourth an $\mathrm{OA}(54,9,3,2)$.
    To obtain these arrays, choose representatives $a_1,\ldots,a_{13}$ of the one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_3^3$ and form the $27$ rows $(x\cdot a_j)_{j=1}^{13}$, for $x\in\mathbb{F}_3^3$.
    Two distinct columns are linearly independent, so every ordered symbol pair occurs three times.  
    Duplicating every row and retaining four or nine columns provides the required arrays.
    The required auxiliary graphs are respectively $30$-regular and $15$-regular on $54$ vertices with spectra $\{[30]^1,[6]^9,[3]^8,[-3]^{36}\}$ and $\{[15]^1,[6]^4,[3]^{18},[-3]^{31}\}$.  
    Having four distinct eigenvalues, neither is strongly regular.  
    Section~\ref{sec:row4-muzychuk} constructs a compatible design and auxiliary graph for the fourth row.  
    The first row remains open: an orthogonal array with the required parameters is available, but a compatible auxiliary graph is not known.
    For this row the complement of an auxiliary graph would have Seidel matrix $I+2A(\Gamma)-J$.  
    Its eigenvalue on $\mathbf1$ is $1+2\cdot30-54=7$, and its eigenvalues on $\mathbf1^\perp$ are $1+2\eta$, where $\eta$ runs through the restricted auxiliary eigenvalues.  
    Its spectrum would therefore be $\{[-5]^{36},[7]^9,[13]^9\}$.
    This Seidel spectrum was considered earlier by the first     author~\cite[Table~2]{LAApaper}.

title: Proposition

\label{pro:specSwitch}
    Let $\sigma$ be an equitable $2$-partition of a graph $\Gamma$.
    Then
    \[
    \operatorname{Spec} \left (A(\Gamma^{\sigma}) \right ) =  \operatorname{Spec}(A(\Gamma)) \cup \operatorname{Spec}(Q_\sigma(\Gamma^{\sigma})) - \operatorname{Spec}(Q_\sigma(\Gamma)) .

label: rem:switch126
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:switch126}
    The third row of Table~\ref{tab:feasible-parameters} is obtained by switching a strongly regular graph $\Delta$ with parameters $(126,45,12,18)$, whose spectrum is $\{[45]^1,[3]^{90},[-9]^{35}\}$.
    For completeness, such a pair $(\Delta,U)$ can be specified in coordinates.  
    Take the standard orthogonal graph $\operatorname{NO}_6^-(3)$ ~\cite{BrouwerVanMaldeghem}: its vertices are the projective points $\langle x\rangle$ with $x\cdot x=1$ in $\mathbb{F}_3^6$, and adjacency is orthogonality for the standard dot product.  
    Let
    \[
        T=\langle e_3+e_4+e_5,\ e_3-e_4+e_6\rangle,
        \qquad
        U_i=\{\langle e_i+t\rangle:t\in T\}\quad(i=1,2).
    \]
    The space $T$ is totally isotropic and perpendicular to $e_1,e_2$.
    Each $U_i$ consists of nine distinct norm-one points.
Since $T$ is totally isotropic and perpendicular to $e_1,e_2$,
\[
    (e_i+s)\cdot(e_j+t)=
    \begin{cases}
        1,& i=j,\\
        0,& i\ne j,
    \end{cases}
    \qquad(s,t\in T;\ i,j\in\{1,2\}).
\]
Thus there are no edges within either $U_i$, and every vertex of $U_1$ is adjacent to every vertex of $U_2$.
Hence $U=U_1\cup U_2$ induces $K_{9,9}=\overline{2K_9}$.
    The partition $\sigma=\{U,V(\Delta)\setminus U\}$ is necessarily equitable.
    Indeed, set $C=A(\Delta)$ and $d_x=|N_\Delta(x)\cap U|$ for $x\notin U$.
    Since $C^2=27I-6C+18J$ and $\Delta[U]$ is $9$-regular, we have
    \[
        \sum_{x\notin U}d_x=18(45-9)=648,\qquad
        \sum_{x\notin U}d_x^2
        =27\cdot18-6\cdot18\cdot9+18\cdot18^2-18\cdot9^2=3888.
    \]
    It follows that $\sum_{x\notin U}(d_x-6)^2=3888-12\cdot648+36\cdot108=0$.
    Thus every vertex outside $U$ has exactly $6$ neighbours in $U$, giving
    \[
        Q_\sigma(\Delta) = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 36 \\ 6 & 39 \end{bmatrix},
        \qquad
        Q_\sigma(\Delta^\sigma) = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 72 \\ 12 & 39 \end{bmatrix},
    \]
    These matrices have spectra $\{45,3\}$ and $\{57,-9\}$, respectively.  
    Hence Proposition~\ref{pro:specSwitch} yields
    \[
        \operatorname{Spec}(A(\Delta^\sigma))=\{[57]^1,[3]^{89},[-9]^{36}\}.
    \]
    Thus $\Delta^\sigma\in\mathscr G_3(57,3,-9)$, with degrees $81$ and $51$.
    Switching does not alter $\Delta[U]$, so $\Delta^\sigma[U] = \overline{2K_9}$ is complete multipartite and Theorem~\ref{thm:2-des} applies, returning a group divisible design with $m = 2$, $n = 9$, $r = 72$, $k = 12$, $\lambda_1 = 72 + 3\cdot(-9) = 45$ and $\lambda_2 = 72 + 4\cdot(-8) - 1 + 9 = 48$, which are the parameters listed.
    Its auxiliary graph is $\Delta[V(\Delta)\setminus U]$, of degree $39$ on $108$ vertices, with spectrum $\{[39]^1,[3]^{73},[-6]^{16},[-9]^{18}\}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:auxSpec}.

label: lem:mult-aux
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:mult-aux}
    Let $\mathcal D$ be a multiplicative semiregular group divisible design and let $\Gamma$ be an auxiliary graph of $\mathcal D$.
    Suppose $\mathcal D$ has parameters $(v,b;r,k;\lambda_1,\lambda_2;m,n)$.
    Then $k_\Gamma=\lambda_1$, or $m>2$ and     $k_\Gamma=\frac{2\lambda_2(v-n)}{v-2n}-\lambda_1$.
    Moreover,
    \begin{equation*}
    m = \frac{k_\Gamma^2-b\,k_\Gamma+n^2(b-1)}{n^2(n-1)}, \qquad x + y = b - 1 - m(n-1), \qquad y - x = \frac{k_\Gamma}{n},
    \end{equation*}
    and, 
    \[
        \operatorname{Spec}(A(\Gamma)) = \left\{ [k_\Gamma]^1,\ [0]^{m(n-1)},\ [n]^{x},\ [-n]^{y} \right\}.
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:auxSpec} with $\theta_1 = n$ and $\theta_2 = -n$, we have the stated spectrum, since $\theta_1+\theta_2 = 0$ and $\theta_1-\theta_2 = 2n$.
Adding and subtracting the expressions for $x$ and $y$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:auxSpec}, one obtains the stated sum and difference.
Since $x$ and $y$ are integers, so is $y-x = k_\Gamma/n$.

By Remark~\ref{rem:degree-compatibility}, $k_\Gamma=\lambda_2-n=\lambda_1$ or
\[
    k_\Gamma=n+\frac{v\lambda_2}{v-2n}
    =\frac{2\lambda_2(v-n)}{v-2n}-\lambda_1.
\]
In the latter case, Remark~\ref{rem:degree-compatibility} also implies $v-n>n$, so $v=mn$ implies $m>2$.

Multiplicativity implies that $\theta_1+\theta_2 = 0$ and $\theta_1^2 = \theta_2^2 = n^2$, so the trace identity of Lemma~\ref{lem:auxSpec} reads $k_\Gamma^2 + n^2(x+y) = bk_\Gamma$; substituting $x+y = b-1-m(n-1)$ and solving for $m$ yields the stated formula.
head: environment

label: prop:s-one
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:s-one}
Let $\mathcal D$ be a multiplicative semiregular GDD with parameters $(v,b;r,k;\lambda_1,\lambda_2;m,n)$ and $s=k/m=1$.
Suppose $\Gamma$ be an auxiliary graph of $\mathcal D$ and $v-n+r\ne k_\Gamma+k$.
Then $\Gamma$ is empty and
\[
    (v,b;r,k;\lambda_1,\lambda_2;m,n)
      =\bigl(n(n^2+n+1),n^3;n^2,n^2+n+1;0,n;n^2+n+1,n\bigr).
\]
head: environment

label: eqn:s1-factor
title: Proof
body_md:
Using \eqref{eqn:params-ns}, we find that $\lambda_1=0$, $\lambda_2=n$, $r=n^2$, $k=m$ and $b=n^3$.
Suppose that $k_\Gamma\ne0$.  
By Lemma~\ref{lem:mult-aux}, we have $m>2$ and $k_\Gamma=2n(m-1)/(m-2)$, and
\eqref{eqn:mult-bireg-branch} becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:s1-factor}
    m^2-(n^2-n+1)m+2n(n-1)=0.
\end{equation}
Its discriminant is $(n^2-n-3)^2-8$.  
This is negative for $n=2$; for $n\geqslant4$ it lies strictly between the consecutive squares $(n^2-n-4)^2$ and $(n^2-n-3)^2$.
Thus $n=3$, and \eqref{eqn:s1-factor} implies $m=3$ or $4$.
If $m=3$, then $k_\Gamma=12$ and both full-graph degrees are $15$, contrary to biregularity.  
If $m=4$, then $k_\Gamma=9$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:mult-aux}, we have $x+y=18$ and $y-x=3$, contrary to integrality of the multiplicities.

Hence $k_\Gamma=0$.  
By Lemma~\ref{lem:mult-aux}, we have $m=(n^3-1)/(n-1)=n^2+n+1$.
Substitution provides the remaining parameters.
head: environment

label: prop:kG-forced
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:kG-forced}
    Let $s\geqslant2$ be an integer, and let $\mathcal D$ be a group divisible design with parameters
    \[
(v,b;r,k;\lambda_1,\lambda_2;m,n)  = (s^2m,\ s^4(s+1);\ s^3(s+1),\ sm;\ s^3,\ s^2(s+1);\ m,\ s^2).
\]
    Suppose $\Gamma$ is an auxiliary graph of $\mathcal D$ and $k_\Gamma\ne s(s-1)m+s^2(s^2+s-1)$.
    Then $k_\Gamma = \lambda_1 = s^3$, $m = s^3+1$, and
    \[
        \operatorname{Spec}(A(\Gamma)) = \Big\{ [s^3]^1,\ [0]^{(s^3+1)(s^2-1)},\
        [s^2]^{\frac{s(s+1)(s^2-1)}{2}},\ [-s^2]^{\frac{s(s+1)(s^2-1)}{2}+s} \Big\} .
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that the nonprincipal quotient eigenvalue is $s^2$.
Taking $n=s^2$ and $\lambda_2=s^2(s+1)$ in \eqref{eqn:mult-bireg-branch}, we have $m^2-(s^3-2s+1)m+2s(s^2-1)=0$.
The discriminant is $D_s=s^6-4s^4-6s^3+4s^2+4s+1$.
For $s=2$ it is negative.  
For $s\geqslant3$, we have $(s^3-2s-4)^2<D_s<(s^3-2s-3)^2$, since the differences are $2s^3-12s-15>0$ and $8(s+1)>0$, respectively. 
Thus $D_s$ is not a square, contradicting $m\in\mathbb{Z}$.

The nonprincipal quotient eigenvalue is therefore $-s^2$.
By Remark~\ref{rem:degree-compatibility}, $k_\Gamma=\lambda_2-s^2=s^3$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:mult-aux}, we have $m=s^3+1$ and
\[
    x+y=s^2(s^2+s-1),\qquad y-x=s.
\]
These yield the stated spectrum.

label: cor:muzychuk-affine-planes
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{cor:muzychuk-affine-planes}
Let $q$ be a prime power and $p=q(q+1)(q^2-1)/2$.
Then
\[
    \operatorname{Spec}(A(G_q))
      =\big\{[q^3]^1,[0]^{(q^2-1)(q^3+1)},
                   [q^2]^p,[-q^2]^{p+q}\big\}.

head: environment

label: lem:kernel-completion
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $A(G_q)\mathbf1=q^3\mathbf1$, \eqref{eqn:family-centred-rows} implies $\left(B-\frac1qJ\right)\mathbf1=0$, and hence $B\mathbf1=q^3(q+1)\mathbf1$.
For the indicator $\mathbf g$ of any one of the $m$ groups, \eqref{eqn:target-centred-gram} implies
\[
    \left\|\left(B-\frac1qJ\right)^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\mathbf g\right\|^2=0.
\]
Hence,
\[
    (I_m\otimes J_{q^2})B=qJ,
    \qquad B^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\mathbf1=qm\mathbf1.
\]
Furthermore, expanding \eqref{eqn:target-centred-gram} using the row sums of $B$ yields
\[
    BB^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 

      =q^4I_v-q^2(I_m\otimes J_{q^2})+(q^3+q^2)J.
\]
These identities give the claimed GDD parameters, which satisfy $r>\lambda_1$ and $rk=v\lambda_2$.
Thus $\mathcal D$ is semiregular.

Let $E_{\ker}$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\ker A(G_q)$.
By \eqref{eqn:target-centred-gram},
\[
    \left(B-\frac1qJ\right)
    \left(B-\frac1qJ\right)^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 

      =q^4\left(I_v-\frac1{q^2}(I_m\otimes J_{q^2})\right).
\]
The matrix in parentheses is an orthogonal projection of rank $m(q^2-1)$.  
Consequently,
\[
    \operatorname{rank}\left(B-\frac1qJ\right)=m(q^2-1),
\]
and all nonzero squared singular values of $B-\frac1qJ$ equal $q^4$.
By \eqref{eqn:family-centred-rows} and the symmetry of $A(G_q)$, the row space of $B-\frac1qJ$ is contained in $\ker A(G_q)$.
By Lemma~\ref{cor:muzychuk-affine-planes}, we have $\dim\ker A(G_q)=m(q^2-1)$.
Thus, $\ker A(G_q)$ is equal to the row space of $B-\frac1qJ$.
It follows that
\[
    \left(B-\frac1qJ\right)^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 

    \left(B-\frac1qJ\right)=q^4E_{\ker}.
\]
Since $B^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\mathbf1=qm\mathbf1$ and $v=mq^2$, we have $\left(B-\frac1qJ\right)^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\mathbf1=0$.
Hence,
\[
    B^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
 B
      =\left(B-\frac1qJ\right)^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 

         \left(B-\frac1qJ\right)+\frac{v}{q^2}J
      =q^4E_{\ker}+(q^3+1)J.
\]

By Lemma~\ref{cor:muzychuk-affine-planes}, we have
\[
    A(G_q)^2=q^4(I_b-E_{\ker})+(q-1)J.
\]
Together with \eqref{eqn:family-centred-rows} and the $q^3$-regularity of $G_q$, these identities imply
\[
    BA(G_q)=q^2J,
    \qquad
    B^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
 B+A(G_q)^2=q^4I_b+(q^3+q)J.
\]
Here $\lambda_2-\lambda_1=n=q^2$, so these are precisely \eqref{eqn:aux-mixed} and \eqref{eqn:aux-block}.
Finally, \eqref{eqn:aux-scalar} becomes
\[
    (q^4+q^2)^2=(q^5+q^3)(q^3+q),
\]
which is satisfied.
Thus $G_q$ is an auxiliary graph for $\mathcal D$.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:main-three}
Let $q$ be a prime power.  
Then $\Gamma_q$ is a connected biregular graph on $2q^5+q^4+q^2$ vertices with degrees $q^5+q^4+q^3$ and $q^4+q^3+q$.

    \{[q^5+q^3+q^2]^1,[q^2]^{f_q},[-q^2]^{g_q}\},

label: lem:row4-clique-size
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:row4-clique-size}
Every clique in $\mathcal H_3$ has size at most $27$.
For a clique of size $27$, the relation defined by inner product $-54$ is the disjoint union of nine triangles.
If $W$ has these clique vectors as its rows, then $M_4=(W+J)/3$ is the incidence matrix of a semiregular GDD with parameters $(27,54;18,9;0,6;9,3)$, with the triangles as its groups.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $W$ have the vectors of an $h$-clique as its rows, and let $D$ be the adjacency matrix of the graph recording inner product $-54$.
Then
\[
    WW^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
=108I_h-54D.
\]
This matrix is positive semidefinite and has rank at most $\dim E_3=18$, so every eigenvalue of $D$ is at most $2$.
In each connected component of $D$, an eigenvalue $2$, if present, is the Perron eigenvalue and is simple.
Such a component has at least three vertices.
The nullity of $108I_h-54D$ is therefore at most $h/3$, whence
\[
    \frac{2h}{3}\leqslant\operatorname{rank}(WW^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
)\leqslant18.
\]
Thus $h\leqslant27$.
If $h=27$, equality forces nine connected components of order three, each with spectral radius $2$; each is therefore a triangle.

Within each triangle, the sum of its three vectors has squared norm $3\cdot108+6(-54)=0$, so that sum is zero.
The three corresponding rows of $(W+J)/3$ therefore sum to $\mathbf1_{54}^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
$.
Thus every column has sum $9$.  
Every row has sum $18$, and the prescribed inner products give intersection $0$ within each group and $6$ between groups.  
These are the stated GDD parameters.
Finally, $18>0$ and $18\cdot9=27\cdot6$, so the design is semiregular.
head: environment

label: thm:row4-muzychuk
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By direct computation
\begin{align*}
    M_4M_4^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 

       &=18I_{27}-6(I_9\otimes J_3)+6J_{27},
          \\
    M_4\mathbf1&=18\mathbf1,\qquad
          M_4^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\mathbf1=9\mathbf1,\\
    M_4A(G)&=3M_4+4J_{27,54},\\
    M_4^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
 M_4+A(G)^2-3A(G)
       &=18I_{54}+6J_{54}.
\end{align*}
The first two lines give the stated GDD parameters, with the indicated groups.  
The design is semiregular since $18>0$ and $18\cdot9=27\cdot6$.
The last two lines are the auxiliary-graph identities; the coefficient of $J_{54}$ in \eqref{eqn:aux-block} is $((15-6)(15+3)+18\cdot9)/54=6$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:gdd-to-3ev} now applies.  
The quotient matrix $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}24&18\\9&15\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ has eigenvalues $33$ and $6$, and its row sums give the two degrees.
The eigenvalue multiplicities follow from the order of $\Gamma_{81}$ and the trace of its adjacency matrix.

label: lem:Cayley
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Cayley}
For each $a\in\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}$, the graph $L_{q,a}$ has spectrum
\[
\operatorname{Spec}(A(L_{q,a})) = \left \{ [q^3-q]^1,\ [q^2-q]^{q(q^2-1)},\ [-q]^{(q-1)(q^3+1)} \right \}.

head: environment

label: lem:eigenmatrix-prime
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:eigenmatrix-prime}
Let $q$ be a prime power. 
Then $\mathcal A_q^\prime$ is a symmetric three-class association scheme with first eigenmatrix
\[
\bbordermatrix{
    & I & \mathsf A_{\neq} & \mathsf A_3 & \mathsf A_4 \endline
  \mathsf E_0 & 1 & q^5 & q^3-q & q^4-q^3+q-1 \endline
  \mathsf E_1 & 1 & -q^4 & q^3-q & q^4-q^3+q-1 \endline
  \mathsf E_2 & 1 & 0 & -q & q-1 \endline
  \mathsf E_3^\prime & 1 & 0 & q^2-q & -q^2+q-1 \endline
}.
\]
The ranks of $\mathsf E_0, \mathsf E_1, \mathsf E_2, \mathsf E_3^\prime$ are $1$, $q$, $(q^2-1)(q^3+1)$ and $q(q+1)(q^2-1)$ respectively. 
Moreover, the column space of $\mathsf E_1$ is spanned by the vectors $\mathbf{g}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{q^4}$ with $\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{q+1}$ and $\sum_a g_a=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:Cayley}, the graphs $L_{q,a}$ are strongly regular with parameters independent of $a$.  
Hence products of the within-copy relations have the same coefficients in every copy.  
Products involving $\mathsf A_{\neq}$ depend only on the common order and valency of these graphs.  
Thus the span of $\mathcal A_q^\prime$ is closed under multiplication, so $\mathcal A_q^\prime$ is a symmetric three-class association scheme.

Its common eigenspaces are the span of $\mathbf1$; the space $\{\mathbf g\otimes\mathbf1_{q^4}:\sum_a g_a=0\}$ of dimension $q$; and the two spaces
\[
    \mathfrak U_1 = \bigoplus_{a\in\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}}\ \bigoplus_{C\in\mathcal F_a}U_a(C),
    \qquad
    \mathfrak U_2 =\bigoplus_{a\in\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}}\ \bigoplus_{C\in\mathcal S_a}U_a(C).
\]
On the copy-constant space orthogonal to $\mathbf1$, the matrices $\mathsf A_{\neq}$ and $\mathsf A_3$ act as $-q^4$ and $q^3-q$, respectively. 
On both the spaces $\mathfrak U_1$ and $\mathfrak U_2$, the matrix $\mathsf A_{\neq}$ acts as zero.
For $C\in\mathcal P$, let $R_{a,C}$ join distinct points of $\Omega_a$ on a common copied line $\{a\}\times L$, where $L\in C$.  
Then $A(L_{q,a})=\sum_{C\in\mathcal S_a}R_{a,C}$.
On $U_a(C')$, the matrix $R_{a,C}$ acts as $q^2-1$ when $C=C'$ and as $-1$ otherwise: lines of distinct classes meet in one point, so a vector in $U_a(C')$ sums to zero on every line of $C$.
Summing over the $q$ used classes, $\mathsf A_3$ therefore acts as $-q$ on the free-class space and as $q^2-q$ on the used-class space.
Their dimensions are $(q+1)(q^2-q+1)(q^2-1)=(q^2-1)(q^3+1)$ and $(q+1)q(q^2-1)$, respectively.
The entries for $\mathsf A_4$ follow from $I + \mathsf A_{\neq}+\mathsf A_3+\mathsf A_4 = J$.
head: environment

label: thm:main-scheme-and-eigenmatrix
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main-scheme-and-eigenmatrix}
Let $q$ be a prime power.
Then $\mathcal A_q$ is a four-class symmetric association scheme whose first eigenmatrix is
\[
\bbordermatrix{
    & I & \mathsf A_1 & \mathsf A_2 & \mathsf A_3 & \mathsf A_4 \endline
  \mathsf E_0 & 1 & q^3 & q^5-q^3 & q^3-q & q^4-q^3+q-1 \endline
  \mathsf E_1 & 1 & -q^2 & q^2-q^4 & q^3-q & q^4-q^3+q-1 \endline
  \mathsf E_2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & -q & q-1 \endline
  \mathsf E_3 & 1 & q^2 & -q^2 & q^2-q & -q^2+q-1 \endline
  \mathsf E_4 & 1 & -q^2 & q^2 & q^2-q & -q^2+q-1 
}.
\]
The ranks of $\mathsf E_0, \mathsf E_1, \mathsf E_2, \mathsf E_3, \mathsf E_4$ are respectively $1$, $q$, $(q^2-1)(q^3+1)$, $\frac{q(q+1)(q^2-1)}{2}$ and $\frac{q(q+1)(q^2-1)}{2}$.
head: environment

label: eqn:A1sq
title: Proof
body_md:
We first verify the products involving $\mathsf A_1$.  
These are instances of the matched parallel-class calculations in \cite[Proposition~2.2]{Muzychuk2007}:
\begin{align}
    \mathsf A_1^2&=q^3I+(q-1)\mathsf A_{\neq}+q^2\mathsf A_3,
        \label{eqn:A1sq}\\
    \mathsf A_1\mathsf A_3&=(q^2-1)\mathsf A_1+(q-1)\mathsf A_2.
        \label{eqn:A1A3}
\end{align}
Every vertex has a line of $q^2$ neighbours in each of the $q$ other copies, so its degree is $q^3$.  
Two distinct vertices in the same copy have common neighbours in another copy precisely when they lie on the same line of the
class assigned to that copy.  
Each selected class is used once, so their number of common neighbours is $q^2$ when their joining line is in a
selected class and zero otherwise.  
For vertices in distinct copies, each of the $q-1$ remaining copies contributes the intersection of two lines from distinct parallel classes, hence one common neighbour.  
This proves \eqref{eqn:A1sq}.

For \eqref{eqn:A1A3}, take vertices $x\in\Omega_a$ and $y\in\Omega_b$, where $a\ne b$.  
The neighbours of $x$ in $\Omega_b$ form a line $L$ in a selected class.  
If $y\in L$, then the $q^2-1$ other points of $L$ are adjacent to $y$ in $L_{q,b}$, and there are no further contributions.  
If $y\notin L$, each of the other $q-1$ selected classes supplies exactly one point of $L$ adjacent to $y$.  
These points are distinct.  
The product is zero when the two vertices lie in the same copy, proving the identity.

Since $\mathsf A_2 = \mathsf A_{\neq} - \mathsf A_1$ and $\mathsf A_4 = J - I - \mathsf A_{\neq} - \mathsf A_3$, and since $\{I, \mathsf A_{\neq}, \mathsf A_3, \mathsf A_4\}$ spans the Bose--Mesner algebra of $\mathcal{A}_q^\prime$, \eqref{eqn:A1sq} and \eqref{eqn:A1A3}, together with
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:A1Ane}
        \mathsf A_1\mathsf A_{\neq}
    =q^3(I+\mathsf A_3+\mathsf A_4)+q^2(q-1)\mathsf A_{\neq},
\end{equation}
show that the span of $\mathcal A_q$ is closed under multiplication.
Here, \eqref{eqn:A1Ane} follows from the fact that every vertex has $q^2$ neighbours in each other copy of $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^2$.
Thus $\mathcal{A}_q$ is a four-class symmetric association scheme.

Now we determine its first eigenmatrix. By \eqref{eqn:A1sq}, each eigenvalue $\theta$ of $\mathsf A_1$ satisfies $\theta^2 = q^3 + (q-1)\alpha + q^2\beta$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the eigenvalues of $\mathsf A_{\neq}$ and $\mathsf A_3$ on the corresponding idempotent of $\mathcal A_q'$.
Using the values of Lemma~\ref{lem:eigenmatrix-prime}, we find
\[
    \mathsf A_1\mathsf E_0=q^3\mathsf E_0,\qquad
    \mathsf A_1^2\mathsf E_1=q^4\mathsf E_1,\qquad
    \mathsf A_1\mathsf E_2=O,\qquad
    \mathsf A_1^2\mathsf E_3^\prime=q^4\mathsf E_3^\prime.
\]
Thus the eigenvalues of $\mathsf A_1$ on the column spaces of $\mathsf E_1$ and $\mathsf E_3^\prime$ lie in $\{q^2,-q^2\}$.

To determine the sign on $\mathsf E_1$, let $\mathbf x = \mathbf g \otimes \mathbf{1}_{q^4}$ with $\sum_{a=0}^q g_a = 0$, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:eigenmatrix-prime}.
By construction, for fixed distinct $a,b$ and fixed $\mathbf v$ there are exactly $q^2$ vectors $\mathbf w$ with $\mathsf A_1[(a,\mathbf v),(b,\mathbf w)] = 1$, so
\[
    (\mathsf A_1 \mathbf x)_{(a,\mathbf v)} = \sum_{b \neq a} q^2 g_b = q^2 \left ( \sum_{b \in \mathbb{Z}_{q+1}} g_b - g_a \right ) = -q^2 g_a .
\]
Hence $\mathsf A_1 \mathsf E_1 = - q^2\mathsf E_1$, and $\mathsf E_1$ does not split.

Consequently the image of $\mathsf E_3^\prime$ decomposes into its $q^2$- and $-q^2$-eigenspaces, of dimensions $m_3,m_4$, initially possibly zero.
Since $\operatorname{tr} \mathsf A_1 = 0$,
\[
    q^3 + q(-q^2) + \operatorname{rank}(\mathsf E_2)\cdot 0 + m_3 q^2 - m_4 q^2 = 0 ,
\]
so $m_3 = m_4$; and $m_3 + m_4 = \operatorname{rank}(\mathsf E_3^\prime) = q(q+1)(q^2-1)$ implies that $m_3 = m_4 = \frac{q(q+1)(q^2-1)}{2}$.

The dimensions are positive, so both eigenspaces occur.  
Their projections are the remaining primitive idempotents $\mathsf E_3,\mathsf E_4$, since the algebra has dimension five.
The remaining entries follow by linearity: since $\mathsf A_2 = \mathsf A_{\neq} - \mathsf A_1$, its eigenvalues are $\alpha - \theta$; and since $\sum_{j=0}^4 \mathsf A_j = J$, the eigenvalues of $\mathsf A_4$ on the non-principal idempotents are $-1 - \theta - (\alpha - \theta) - \beta = -1 - \alpha - \beta$.
head: environment

label: cor:auxiliary-coherent-rank
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:auxiliary-coherent-rank}
Let $q$ be a prime power.
Then
\[
    \mathcal W(G_q)
      =\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{I,\mathsf A_1,\mathsf A_2,
                                    \mathsf A_3,\mathsf A_4\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:main-scheme-and-eigenmatrix} the coherent closure $\mathcal W(G_q)$ is contained in $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{I,\mathsf A_1,\mathsf A_2,                                    \mathsf A_3,\mathsf A_4\}$.  
    To prove the reverse inclusion, put $H=\mathsf A_1^2-q^3I$.
By \eqref{eqn:A1sq}, $H=(q-1)\mathsf A_{\neq}+q^2\mathsf A_3$.
Since $\mathsf A_{\neq}$ and $\mathsf A_3$ have disjoint binary supports,
\[
    \mathsf A_3=
       \frac{H\circ H-(q-1)H}{q^2(q^2-q+1)},
    \qquad
    \mathsf A_{\neq}=\frac{H-q^2\mathsf A_3}{q-1}.
\]
Both matrices therefore belong to $\mathcal W(G_q)$.
The identities
\[
    \mathsf A_2=\mathsf A_{\neq}-\mathsf A_1,
    \qquad
    \mathsf A_4=J-I-\mathsf A_{\neq}-\mathsf A_3
\]
show that the remaining basis matrices also belong to the coherent closure.  
This proves equality.
head: environment

label: lem:degree-block-rank
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:degree-block-rank}
Let $\Gamma$ be a biregular graph with degree partition $\{V_1,V_2\}$.
Let $G_i=\Gamma[V_i]$ for $i=1,2$.
Suppose $A(\Gamma) = \left [\begin{smallmatrix}A(G_1)&B\\B^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
&A(G_2)\end{smallmatrix}\right ]$, where $B\notin\{O,J\}$.
Then
\[
    \operatorname{cr}(\Gamma)\geqslant
    \operatorname{cr}(\Gamma[V_1])+\operatorname{cr}(\Gamma[V_2])+4.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $A=A(\Gamma)$ and let $d_1\ne d_2$ be the two degrees.  
The diagonal matrix $D=A^2\circ I$ belongs to $\mathcal W(\Gamma)$, so the diagonal indicator matrices
\[
    F_1=\frac{D-d_2I}{d_1-d_2},\qquad F_2=I-F_1
\]
of $V_1,V_2$ belong to it.  
Restricted to $V_i\times V_i$, the corner $F_i\mathcal W(\Gamma)F_i$ is a coherent algebra containing $A(\Gamma[V_i])$.
Its dimension is therefore at least $\operatorname{cr}(\Gamma[V_i])$.  
Each off-diagonal corner contains the two linearly independent matrices $B,J_{|V_1|,|V_2|}$ or their transposes.
The four corners have disjoint supports, so their dimensions add, giving the stated bound.
head: environment

label: prop:family-coherent-type
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $m=q^3+1$, $v=mq^2$, $b=q^4(q+1)$.  
The adjacency matrix of $\Gamma_q$ is
\[
    A=\begin{bmatrix}J_v-I_m\otimes J_{q^2}&M_q\\M_q^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
&\mathsf A_1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
By Corollary~\ref{cor:main-three}, its point and block sets are its two degree classes.  
We exhibit a coherent algebra of dimension $12$ containing $A$, then apply Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-block-rank} to prove that it is the coherent closure.

Let
\[
\begin{gathered}
    \mathcal L=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{I_v,I_m\otimes J_{q^2},J_v\},\qquad
    \mathcal U=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{M_q,J_{v,b}\},\\
    \mathcal R=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}
       \{I_b,\mathsf A_1,\mathsf A_2,\mathsf A_3,\mathsf A_4\}.
\end{gathered}
\]
Here $\mathcal L$ is the rank-three Bose--Mesner algebra of the complete multipartite graph on the points, and $\mathcal R$ is the rank-five coherent closure of the auxiliary graph by Corollary~\ref{cor:auxiliary-coherent-rank}.

Since $G_q$ is an auxiliary graph of $\mathcal D_q$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-completion}, we can apply \eqref{eqn:aux-block} to obtain
\[
    M_q^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
 M_q=q^4I+(q^3+q)J-\mathsf A_1^2.
\]
Using \eqref{eqn:A1sq} and $J=I+\mathsf A_{\neq}+\mathsf A_3+\mathsf A_4$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:MtM}
    M_q^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
 M_q=(q^4+q)I+(q^3+1)\mathsf A_{\neq}
       +(q^3-q^2+q)\mathsf A_3+(q^3+q)\mathsf A_4.
\end{equation}

To check multiplication across the two degree classes, we use
\begin{align*}
    M_q\mathsf A_1&=q^2J,&
    M_q\mathsf A_2&=(q^4-q^2)J,\\
    M_q\mathsf A_3&=-qM_q+q^2J,&
    M_q\mathsf A_4&=(q-1)M_q+(q^3-q^2)J.
\end{align*}
The first identity follows from \eqref{eqn:aux-mixed}. 
Every row of $M_q$ has $q^3$ ones in each copy, so $M_q\mathsf A_{\neq}=q^4J$, giving the second.  
For the third, each of the $q$ used-class lines through a fixed vertex meets the row's $q$ selected free-class lines in $q$
points.  
Removing the vertex itself subtracts $q$ precisely when its incidence entry is one, giving $q^2-qM_q$.  
Since $I+\mathsf A_3+\mathsf A_4$ is the block-diagonal matrix with one all-ones block for each copy, and every row of $M_q$ has $q^3$ ones in each copy, we have
\[
    M_q(I+\mathsf A_3+\mathsf A_4)=q^3J.
\]
Using the third identity, we obtain
\[
    M_q\mathsf A_4
      =q^3J-M_q-M_q\mathsf A_3
      =(q-1)M_q+(q^3-q^2)J.
\]
These four identities show that $M_qR\in\mathcal U$ for every $R\in\mathcal R$.  
Since each such $R$ has constant column sum, we also have $JR\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{J\}$.
As $\mathcal U=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{M_q,J\}$, it follows that $\mathcal U\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal U$.

By Remark~\ref{rem:semireg}, we have $(I_m\otimes J_{q^2})M_q=qJ$.
Together with the constant row and column sums of $M_q$, one obtains $\mathcal L\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal U$.
By \eqref{eqn:inc}, we have $\mathcal U\mathcal U^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\subseteq\mathcal L$, and by \eqref{eqn:MtM}, we have $\mathcal U^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal R$.
Thus
\[
    \mathcal C=
    \left\{\begin{bmatrix}L&U\\V&R\end{bmatrix}:
       L\in\mathcal L,\ U\in\mathcal U,\
       V\in\mathcal U^ 
  {\mathpalette\@transpose{}} 
,\ R\in\mathcal R\right\},
\]
with its four blocks chosen independently, is closed under ordinary multiplication and transpose.  
It is also closed under Schur multiplication: its disjoint binary basis consists of $I_v,I_m\otimes J_{q^2}-I_v,J_v-I_m\otimes J_{q^2}$ on the point side, $I_b,\mathsf A_1,\ldots,\mathsf A_4$ on the block side, and $M_q,J-M_q$ and their transposes between the two sides, each extended by zero outside its corner.  
These twelve matrices are nonzero, and $\mathcal C$ contains $I,J,A$.  
Hence $\mathcal W(\Gamma_q)\subseteq\mathcal C$ and $\dim\mathcal C=12$.

The induced point graph has coherent rank $3$, and the induced block graph has coherent rank $5$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:auxiliary-coherent-rank}.  
Also $M_q\notin\{O,J\}$ by its row sums.  
By Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-block-rank}, we have $\operatorname{cr}(\Gamma_q)\geqslant3+5+4=12$.
It follows that $\mathcal W(\Gamma_q)=\mathcal C$.
Its two diagonal basis relations are the identities on the point and block sets, giving the asserted fibres and type.
